transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-30
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Ava Martinez (Redwood AE), Samir Khan (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Lumina CTO), Ethan Park (Lumina Lead ML Eng), Rita Gomez (Lumina PM)

[00:00] Ava: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, happy holidays too. I'm Ava from Redwood, I handle partnerships for retail accounts. Samir and Lena are on from our solutions team, they'll run the product walkthrough. Uh, Maya, Ethan, Rita, thanks for coming.
[00:10] Maya: Thanks, yeah appreciate it. We're curious mostly about latency and cost tradeoffs, and also security — we have some pcard data so residency and logs matter.
[00:18] Samir: Totally, we'll cover those. Today we'll demo the Hosted API flows for chat and text generation — streaming, param tuning like temperature/top_p/max_tokens, stop sequences, and retry/idempotency patterns. We'll also show the Redwood Console quick dashboards and Optimize suggestions for batching/caching.
[00:32] Rita: Sounds good. Also, do you support function calling and structured JSON outputs? We need deterministic-ish outputs for checkout flows.
[00:40] Lena: Yes, function/tool calling is supported in the hosted runtime; you can define schemas and Redwood will return structured responses. We'll show a small example.

[01:05] -- demo begins, Samir shares screen (console.redwood.ai — note: sharing link) --
[01:20] Samir: This is the API docs page — typical REST endpoint /v1/chat and /v1/generate, streaming via chunked HTTP or SSE. If you want streaming, you set stream=true; you'll get partial tokens back as they generate which reduces perceived latency.
[01:40] Ethan: For streaming, does the SDK reassemble partial tokens or do we handle assembly?
[01:47] Samir: SDKs reassemble for common clients; for custom clients you can concatenate chunks. Keep in mind tokens can be split mid-word in transcripts sometimes, so we recommend client-side buffering for final output.

[02:20] Samir: On params, common knobs: temperature (0-1), top_p, max_tokens, frequency_penalty, presence_penalty. For deterministic responses use temp=0 and top_p=0. If you want more creative product descriptions, bump temp to .7 and maybe top_p=.9.
[02:40] Maya: Do you have recommended defaults to balance quality and cost?
[02:45] Samir: Yup — for most retrieval-augmented chat we recommend temp=0.2, top_p=0.9, and max_tokens set to expected reply size. Also Redwood Optimize will suggest quantization or batching changes based on your pattern to lower per-token cost.

[03:20] Lena: Quick note on rate limits and retries — Hosted API enforces per-account rate limits. For transient 429s we recommend exponential backoff with jitter and include our idempotency key header (x-request-id or Idempotency-Key) to avoid double-cost on retries.
[03:38] Ethan: If a request times out server-side, will retry double-bill?
[03:43] Samir: If you use an idempotency key, the runtime will dedupe duplicate in-flight requests, so only one model invocation is billed. Without it, retries may invoke multiple calls.

[04:10] -- Samir pulls up a simple curl example --
[04:20] Samir: curl -X POST /v1/chat -H 'Authorization: Bearer ...' -d '{"stream": true, "messages": [...], "temperature":0.2}' — the streaming chunks come as data: events. We demoed reconnects behaving gracefully; client should rehydrate conversation state and use prefix/KV caching to avoid re-sending long context.

[05:00] Maya: You mentioned prefix/KV cache, how is that handled in hosted mode?
[05:08] Lena: Redwood maintains a per-session KV cache for decoder key-values to speed next-token generation on warm sessions. For hosted we do automatic prefix caching for repeated prompts; for Dedicated or Private you get more control over cache TTL and size.

[06:00] -- brief latency benchmark slide (Samir) --
[06:10] Samir: Here are median latencies by model at 128 token outputs, on our hosted fleet. We show t50/t95. For lighter models t50 can be sub-100ms per token, for larger cross-attention models t95 jumps; we include a cost-per-1k-tokens row so you can reason about unit economics.
[06:35] Ethan: What's the tail like under burst? If we get 200 qps spikes, will you autoscale or throttle?
[06:43] Samir: Hosted autoscaling handles typical spikes but there are cold-starts; we offer burst capacity guarantees for enterprise accounts. If you need strict SLO we suggest Dedicated.

[07:10] Rita: On security — logs, data retention, and encryption?
[07:17] Ava: Hosted keeps request/response logs for X days by default, you can configure retention windows, and we offer workspace-level log redaction. All data in transit is TLS; at rest we use KMS-managed keys, and for Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS/HSM. We'll send the SOC2/ISO artifact pack after the call.

[08:00] -- demo: function calling & structured output example --
[08:15] Lena: Here's a schema for a checkout action, we call the model with function schema and it'll return JSON matching that schema. If model returns free-form we can auto-validate and fallback to a parser or graylist.
[08:35] Ethan: Any guidance on reducing hallucinations in structured outputs?
[08:40] Samir: Use stronger guidance: provide examples, set temp lower, and use retrieval or deterministic post-processing validations. Also Redwood Optimize can flag regression in quality over time tied to prompt sets.

[09:20] -- Console tour: routes, token breakdown, Optimize suggestions --
[09:30] Samir: Console shows per-route token cost, latency heatmaps, and an Optimize tab that suggests batching, model quantization, and cache TTL changes. For example it suggested switching to 4-bit quantized variant for our e-commerce SKU generator and increasing batch window by 20ms to save 30% cost without hitting p95.
[10:05] Maya: Does Optimize do automatic rollouts?
[10:08] Lena: You can approve recommendations and do canary rollouts — A/B splits at the routing layer. We also have automatic fallback if quality metrics dip.

[11:00] -- discussion: retry semantics and idempotency detailed --
[11:08] Samir: When using exponential backoff, try 100ms base with doubling and jitter up to 2s; for long-running completions use streaming heartbeats so clients see progress and avoid blind retries. We recommend Idempotency-Key on any non-idempotent operation (like payment confirmation generation).

[12:00] Ethan: Will you support burst token-level concurrency for large responses like 2k tokens?
[12:04] Samir: Yes, but note longer sequences increase memory pressure. We provide guidance to chunk responses where possible or use progressive output. For very long context you can move older context to embeddings store and do retrieval to keep context window reasonable.

[14:00] -- Q&A about pricing & POC --
[14:10] Ava: For POC we often recommend a 2-week pilot on Hosted with limited quota so we can benchmark your QPS and tail latencies; we'll instrument with tracing hooks so you can measure real latency and cost.
[14:25] Maya: That would help. Also need to run a security review — will you give us a remediation plan if we find gaps?
[14:30] Ava: Yes we'll work through security SC with our compliance team; we'll include SOC2 docs and the private deploy options.

[15:00] -- wrap up, recap --
[15:05] Ava: Quick recap: we'll send pricing + hosted/dedicated comparison, security pack, and propose a POC scoping meeting. Samir will own the scoping call and technical onboarding. Ethan will send a sample workload. Any final Qs?
[15:18] Maya: No, thanks, that was helpful.
[15:22] Ethan: Thanks, appreciate the detail.
[15:25] Ava: Great, we'll follow up via email with links to the deck and benchmark sheet (links: https://redwood.ai/decks/lumina-poc and https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/lumina-sample).
[15:35] -- meeting ends --
notes: Customer emphasizes latency & data residency — likely candidate for Dedicated if SLOs tighten
Ethan to provide real workload which will feed Redwood Optimize recommendations
Security pack requested (SOC2/ISO, KMS options, log retention)
